before.label: History of science
before.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.
before.representative_figures_and_works: George Sarton; Alexandre Koyré, Études galiléennes (1939); Robert K. Merton; Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962); Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985). Yates and Foucault provide additional, distinct contributions; they do not substitute for these historians and programmes. Further approaches include Metzger’s history of chemistry (1923), Maier’s medieval natural philosophy (1949), Fleck’s scientific fact (1935), Needham’s collaborative Chinese science project (from 1954), Rossiter’s Women Scientists in America (1982), and Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980).

post.internal_distinctions: Seven new approaches distinguish imperial knowledge, representation, provincializing, colonial nationalism, ambivalence, feminist difference and colonial race/sexuality. Mohanty’s qualified criticism is not rendered as a monolithic opposition between Western and Third World women.

subaltern.people: Expanded three selections to eight. Amin gains a contextual work; Chatterjee and Spivak are reused; Pandey, Prakash and Sarkar added. Spivak and Sarkar have critic roles, and Sarkar’s participant account preserves early achievements and internal disagreement. Regional coverage remains selective.
subaltern.works_and_arguments: Guha’s 1982 statement complements the 1983 book; Amin’s 1995 work joins judicial records to interviews. Chakrabarty’s labor study and 1997 article address different questions. Pandey’s original Oxford 1990 edition is separated from later publisher material; Prakash’s 1999 science history remains within scope.
subaltern.internal_distinctions: Eight approaches separate popular politics, local memory, labor, historical translation, nation/community, gender/representation, colonial science and internal criticism. Guha’s popular autonomy is an argued distinction with overlap and regional variation, rather than an uncontested social fact.
subaltern.incoming_connections: Sarkar’s primary pp. 82–83 give participant evidence of Gramsci and British Marxist reception, including named Thompson references. Spivak supplies a specific gendered criticism. The already recorded labor and peasant-politics interventions retain their qualifications. No generic structuralist influence is added from an unexamined borrowing.
subaltern.outgoing_connections: Added Amin’s contribution to memory inquiry, Prakash’s colonial-science intervention and Chakrabarty’s explicit engagement with Telling the Truth About History. Clarified the critique of elite liberation narratives and the changing relationship to postcolonial scholarship. Neither all liberation histories nor all secular history are treated as one position.
